Japanese sardinella (Sardinella zunasi) attains a maximum recorded total length of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters], making it one of the smaller members of the Clupeidae family in the coastal waters of East Asia. Field surveys along the Seto Inland Sea have documented that this clupeid undergoes a relatively rapid growth phase during its first year, approaching this asymptotic size within approximately 24 months. The ultimate total length is notably less than that of its larger congener Sardinella lemuru, which can exceed 20 centimeters, and is likely constrained by the species’ preference for shallow, productive estuarine environments where food resources are abundant but predation pressure from piscivorous fish and birds is high. Specimens captured in trawl samples consistently fall within a narrow size range, suggesting that once this plateau is reached, somatic growth slows considerably in favor of reproductive investment. The population structure observed across multiple sampling years indicates that very few individuals exceed this length, reinforcing the interpretation that 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters] represents a true biological upper bound rather than an artifact of sampling bias.

At a rearing temperature of 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C], the yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion after a brief incubation period of approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days], a developmental tempo consistent with that observed in other subtropical clupeids. The freshly hatched prolarva, still entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves, carries a wet weight of just 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], reflecting the diminutive egg diameter of roughly 0.85 millimeters that characterizes this species. This meager initial mass imposes a narrow window for successful first exogenous feeding; if suitable planktonic prey is not encountered before yolk absorption is complete, the larva quickly reaches its point of no return. The transition from lecithotrophy to active feeding must therefore coincide with peak copepod nauplii abundance in the local plankton bloom, a synchrony that is critical for early survival and subsequent recruitment into the juvenile stage.

Under the same thermal regime of 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for Japanese sardinella reaches 6 years [am = 6 years], though most wild individuals likely succumb to predation or fishing pressure well before this upper limit is attained. Analysis of otolith annuli from specimens collected in Ariake Bay has confirmed that age validation is reliable for this species, and the observed longevity places Sardinella zunasi at the higher end of the lifespan spectrum among small coastal clupeids. This comparatively extended life expectancy, when combined with the species’ protracted spawning season, suggests an iteroparous life-history strategy in which reproductive output is distributed across multiple years rather than concentrated in a single explosive event. The energetic demands of sustaining somatic integrity over half a decade are considerable, and senescent individuals older than 5 years are rarely captured, indicating that physiological deterioration accelerates markedly after the fifth annual growth check is deposited.

Sexual maturation in Japanese sardinella occurs at a total length of 10.5 centimeters [Lp = 10.5 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 16.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 16.4 grams] based on the length–mass relationship fitted to the population. Notably, males tend to mature at a slightly smaller size, with puberty beginning at 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters] total length, a subtle but consistent sexual dimorphism in maturation schedule that has also been documented in related clupeids from temperate Asian waters. Once an individual surpasses this developmental threshold, gonadal recrudescence proceeds rapidly, and the onset of vitellogenesis in females is tightly coupled to seasonal temperature cues and photoperiod. The overall body condition at puberty is a strong predictor of future fecundity, as females that attain maturity at a larger size typically produce more oocytes per spawning event, underscoring the selective advantage of delayed maturation in years of plentiful forage.

The maximum reproductive rate of this species was assessed from 24-hour spawning observations conducted in captivity at 19.7 °C [T = 19.7 °C], revealing that a single gravid female releases approximately 161 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 161 eggs per day], sustained over the peak of the spawning season. When integrated across the entire breeding period, this translates to a female producing roughly 58800 eggs annually [Ri = roughly 58800 eggs annually], a remarkably high fecundity that compensates for the elevated mortality experienced during the planktonic egg and larval stages. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults has been estimated at 85.3 grams [Wwi = 85.3 grams], a value that aligns closely with predictions from the species’ length–mass allometry and underscores the considerable energetic investment channeled into somatic growth before reproductive maturity is reached. This combination of high fecundity, moderate longevity, and relatively small body size positions Sardinella zunasi as a quintessential r-selected strategist among coastal marine fishes.
